When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking.

"I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says.

But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling.

"The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time."

Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school.

Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data – and that number has risen year-on-year.

When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes.

Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS.

Gracey says the thought of quitting her vape scares her

So why are people like Gracey, who have never smoked a cigarette, taking it up?

The Londoner believes vaping helps when she's feeling socially anxious.

"It's the hand action," she says, "just having something in your hand, just having something in your mouth."

Like cigarettes Gracey's vape contains nicotine, a highly addictive substance that triggers withdrawal symptoms like irritability and anxiety when it leaves your system.

Vaping has become a "mindless action," she says. When she answers the call to talk to BBC News for this article, Gracey says that without thinking about it, she had been lying in bed, with her vape in one hand, and her other hand scrolling Instagram.

The habitual aspect of regular vaping is something GP Dr Helen Wall hears a lot from her patients.

"It's that kind of psychological dependence on something else to almost regulate their emotions," she says.

Like Gracey, Malin Andersson, who vaped until recently, says her habit went hand in hand with doomscrolling.

She had also tried cigarettes but never considered herself a smoker.

At 33, she falls in the age range most likely to vape. The ONS report suggests nearly one in six people aged 25-34 in the UK may use e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.

The domestic abuse campaigner and former Love Island contestant started vaping when she was going through a stressful break-up and looking for comfort. She believes it was the physical action that got her hooked.

"It's a dopamine hit," Malin says. "It's literally an adult's version of a dummy."

She says it was dulling her senses and leaving her demotivated.

Malin became so frustrated with how reliant she had become on her banana ice-flavoured vape that she quit in May this year.

"It was annoying me so much that it was always in my hand that I'd end up throwing it across the room," she says.

Malin said she believed her mental and physical health had improved since quitting vaping in May

Alex, from Manchester, also gradually formed a vaping habit, which started after she occasionally vaped on nights out and then began to take the vapes home.

The 26-year-old, who didn't want to give her last name, says the habit would become such a constant part of her life that she would work while "lying in my bed with my laptop in front of me and then my vape on my chest".

Prof Sarah Jackson, from the University College London Alcohol and Tobacco Research Group, points out that while "alarm bells" may ring at the recent ONS figures, it could be the case that some of the people in this group would have started smoking if they hadn't started vaping.

"In which case, vaping has diverted them away from a more harmful behaviour, which is good news," she says. "On the other hand, there will be people that are being exposed to more risk than they would have otherwise."

She points to a 2024 study from UCL researchers that found nicotine use had risen among young adults in England, although cigarette smoking had declined.

"We can infer from that that some of the people who are vaping wouldn't have smoked otherwise," Jackson says.

The ONS report says about 5.4 million people aged 16 and over vape in Britain, while the number of smokers of all ages continues to steadily fall. Some 4.9 million adults in the UK smoke.

The UK is aiming to cut smoking rates and reduce the appeal of vaping among children and young people.

The marketing of vapes - which has featured bright colours and sweet flavours - is being looked at, with a recent government consultation on new measures expected to give a response in due course.

Within the 1.1 million vapers who never smoked, "there probably is a group who would not be vaping [without] the marketing of vaping which is very prominent", says Hazel Cheeseman from charity Action on Smoking and Health.

The NHS warns non-smokers and those aged 17 and under to never vape, while it's illegal for anyone under 18 to buy vapes. Disposable vapes - seen as a key driver in the rise of youth vaping – were banned last year .

Gracey says she buys a refillable vape at a cost of £5 every day

Wall says the heavy marketing of vapes in recent years has helped to fuel a "misconception" that they are "safe and not addictive".

Gracey thinks vapes should be sold in the same standardised plain packaging as cigarettes because it "looks scary".

"With vapes, they have all these flavours, all these pretty colours - it's just making us more attracted to it".

While she says vaping is seen as far more socially acceptable among her generation than smoking, she finds her habit problematic and has considered quitting to save the £35 a week it costs her.

But just like smoking, giving up vaping can be a struggle. And for Alex, vaping led her in the opposite direction.

She says she managed to quit vaping while travelling for several months, but with no access to vapes she began smoking cigarettes for the first time instead.

Cigarettes are not considered a healthy or helpful way to stop vaping by experts. The NHS strongly advises people to stop smoking, and it remains the leading cause of preventable illness and premature death in the UK.

To quit vaping the NHS suggests gradually reducing the strength of the vape's nicotine, increasing the time between vaping sessions, or switching to a suitable nicotine replacement therapy product.

But professional support to stop vaping is patchy, with a recent survey , external finding fewer than half (45%) of healthcare providers in England offered vaping cessation support. There is a mixed picture of support to quit across the rest of the UK.

While it is good fewer people are smoking, Wall says that for people like Gracey who go straight to vapes a bit of the messaging has been missed. "Vaping was only intended [by the NHS] to be a replacement for cigarettes."

Irene Breen told the BBC her business suffered a significant financial hit from the restrictions

When Irene Breen got a notification in January 2025 that Instagram was removing adverts for her company's pregnancy pillows, she was confused. What was so offensive about a pillow?

She was later told on a call with Meta that the problem was the word "pregnancy".

"We had to scrub the word from our entire website… from the product name," Breen said. "We had to remove all our URLs which had pregnancy in them and rename them all."

The restrictions were eventually lifted but, she said, it took 10 months of conversations with Instagram's parent company Meta - by which time her business had suffered a significant financial hit.

Meta, which also owns Facebook, told the BBC that while businesses can run adverts that promote wellness, sexual health and reproductive products and services, there are restrictions to avoid users across countries and cultures having a negative experience.

The company initially declined to comment on individual cases. After the BBC’s story was published, a spokesperson added: “The suggestion that the word 'pregnancy' cannot be used on our platforms is incorrect. To be clear, people can freely use the word 'pregnancy' in posts, and share and discuss pregnancy-related content.”

It's not just businesses taking out paid adverts who claim their content has been unfairly restricted.

Women's health creators and charities have told us their content has been removed, had sensitivity filters added, or had its reach suppressed - a practice known as "shadowbanning".

The campaign group CensHERship monitors claims that women's health content is being suppressed.

In a report last month, it surveyed nearly 200 creators, clinical providers, health brands, charities, and educators - 96% of whom said they had experienced restrictions in some form.

The fight to say 'vagina' on social media

Sensitivity filters heavily blur posts requiring users to press a button before they can see it and are usually reserved for graphic imagery - including nudity or violence.

Dr Carolina Are, a digital criminologist at the London School of Economics who studies social media moderation of women's content, said research shows AI is often used to flag posts that might breach platform guidelines.

But that can mean an "algorithm misdetecting" content, as it is created to do, storing that information to repeat "previous mistaken decisions", she warns.

The system often uses automated messages, Are says, which can mean users are then unable to question a decision.

Some hashtags just don't appear on Instagram, said Athena Lamnisos, CEO of gynaecological cancer charity Eve Appeal.

"One of the hashtags, unbelievably, was #vaginalcancer."

"We put a post on Instagram about vulval anatomy - it was very clearly an anatomical diagram with labels around it, talking about vulval cancer and the need to check for changes, lumps and bumps. It was pulled."

The diagram was put behind a sensitivity filter

The charity appealed, which was initially denied - but after several weeks the post "suddenly reappeared" behind a sensitivity filter.

Lamnisos added it wasn't exaggerating to say that "life-saving health information isn't getting to the people who need it most".

Despite her raising this with Meta, the problem has continued, she said.

Deirdre O'Neill, from fertility test company Hertility, said it had a similar issue with a Facebook and Instagram video featuring a woman with endometriosis.

"She doesn't sell our services, she doesn't talk about Hertility, she simply describes her pain," O'Neill said.

But the video was removed by Meta, she said, and classified as political content.

Asked about Eve Appeal and Hertility's cases, Meta did not comment specifically, but said it allows women's health content on its platforms, and is consulting with women's health organisations to improve systems.

The post featuring a woman talking about endometriosis was flagged and classified as "social issues, elections or politics"

Trying to advertise on TikTok has also become "like an obstacle course", O'Neill added.

"It's so much resource to try and put something forward that it ends up not being worth our time, because everything gets appealed, flagged, removed," she said.

The advert was returned to Bella Moon with the word "pregnancy" crossed out

TikTok said while certain content can't be promoted on the For You feed, it's transparent about posts that fall into this category and lets creators know so they can appeal.

It added that millions of women share health stories on the platform, including with hashtags like #Period and #Endometriosis.

CensHERship found the number of respondents self-censoring as a result of shadowbanning had gone up, from 53% in 2025 to 65% this year.

This includes using euphemistic terms such as "seggs" instead of "sex", using asterisks or emojis, and avoiding certain topics altogether.

CensHERship co-founder Clio Wood said this was "really damaging", because "women's health historically has been surrounded by shame and guilt… and we are just reinforcing [that]".

Are told the BBC that platforms' policies "tend to be incredibly broad, whereby more often than not, nudity is conflated with sexual activity".

And this ultimately hurts audiences, Wood said.

"We talk to so many people who say, 'The only reason I found out about my vulval cancer was because Eve Appeal posted about those symptoms, and then I researched it and could ask my doctor the right questions'," she said.

But Wood said that, since starting CensHERship in 2024, she has noticed that social media companies "can see this is something that they need to engage on now.".

"It's all very well the policy saying XYZ content is allowed, but if the algorithm is still flagging all of that content and suppressing it, that's where the problem comes in," she said.

"I think within the platforms those departments are very siloed - so what we would love is for those conversations to be much more holistic."

Umuhanzikazi Nyiranyamibwa Suzanne akaba n’umuririmbyi w’inararibonye yapfuye kuri uyu wa Gatanu tariki 16 Ukwakira 2026, azize uburwayi.

Nyiranyamibwa yari umuhanzi ubimazemo imyaka myinshi, wamamaye cyane mu itorero Isamaza no mu ndirimbo zo kwibuka abazize Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi mu 1994.

Azwi cyane mu yitwa ‘Ese mbaze’, ‘’Ndavunyisha’, ‘Nkumbuye iwacu’, ‘Nimuberwe bakobwa’, ‘Ituze’, ‘Telefone’ n’izindi zakanyujijeho.

Nyiranyamibwa yavukiye mu Rwanda ariko aza kuhava mu 1973 ahunze itoteza n’ubwicanyi bwakorerwaga Abatutsi nyuma y’uko se yishwe aroshywe mu ruzi rwa Rusumo mu mwaka wa 1963.

Nyiranyamibwa ni umwe mu baririmbyi b’imena bashinze itorero Isamaza ryagize uruhare rukomeye mu gutiza umurindi ingabo za RPA ku rugamba rwo kubohora u Rwanda.

Mu butumwa bwanditswe na Minisitiri w’Ubumwe bw’Abanyarwanda n’Inshangano Mbonera Gihugu, Dr. Bizimana Jean Damascene , yavuze ko Suzanne Nyiranyamibwa atabarutse akunzwe, yarahojeje abatagira ingano amarira y’agahinda n’akababaro u Rwanda rwatewe na Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi.

Ati “ Ndakwibuka nk’ejo mu minsi ijana yo kwibuka Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi, utaramye uhoza abababaye, uririmbira abatahutse barimbuwe bazizwa uko baremwe. Tuzagukumbura Nyiranyamibwa mwiza.”

Akomeza agira ati “ Ndakwibuka mu ndirimbo zawe z’imena n’urumenesha zashyuhije urugamba rwo kubohora u Rwanda. Ubwira inyangabirama uti “Turaje tuje tujya iwacu, cyo nimusase bugari, dore igihe kirageze, cyo gushyira hamwe twese tugakorera u Rwanda. Turaje muturebe mutumenye turi bene mugabo umwe. Turaje nta rwango ku mutima, nta nzika z’ibyahise. Turaje tubafitiye amakuru n’amajyambere y’ukuri, n’umurava n’ubupfura, ntabwo tuje gusahura, turaje turukumbuye cyane, turukorere buhanga.” Iyo Leta ya Habyarimana wabwiraga ikumva ntimene amaraso, u Rwanda ruba rwemye rutarira amarira y’agahinda ka Jenoside.”

Minisitiri Bizimana yavuze ko Nyiranyamibwa uko imyaka yahitaga yaririmbye indirimbo z’ikizere zikomeza abato n’abakuru.

Ati “ Ikiriyo cyo kwibuka abacu kireka kuba umwanya wo gushavura no kuganya, gihinduka igitaramo cyo kurata ibigwi byaranze abatutsi bishwe n’indangagaciro zabaranze, turushaho kubabera aho batari twemye.”

Akomeza agira ati “Mu myaka yose uko wabishoboye, ibice byose by’u Rwanda wabizengurukaga ujya kwibuka Abatutsi bishwe muri jenoside no gukomeza abakiriho. Wateye benshi ishema, uha benshi imbaraga zo kubaho, bakibuka badashavuye, ihungabana urarihungeta. “

Ygaragaraje ko kandi uyu munyabigwi yahojeje abashavuye i Nyanza na Nyarubuye, Nyamata na Ntarama, Gisozi n’Umujyi wose wa Kigali, Murambi na Bisesero, Mibirizi na Kabgayi, Rukumberi na Kibeho, Kiziguro na Komini Rouge, Mwulire na Musha, Kansi na Kabakobwa, Cyanika na Cyahinda, Kaduha na Gatagara, Songa na Busogo

Ati “Mubyeyi Nyiranyambirwa Suzana, udusigiye icyuho ariko humura ugiye ukeye, ikivi cyawe tuzacyusa.”

KIGALI – APR FC have been urged to deliver another strong performance when they host Egyptian giants Zamalek SC in the CAF Champions League on this Friday evening, with Rwanda Defence Force Chief of Defence Staff Gen. Mubarakh Muganga calling on the players to give fans a reason to celebrate.

Gen. Muganga, who also serves as the club’s Vice Honorary President, made the call on Thursday evening during a visit to the team’s final training session ahead of the first-leg encounter at Amahoro Stadium in Kigali.

He was accompanied by Maj. Gen. Alex Kagame, Chief of the Reserve Force, as the army-owned club prepared for the second-round tie against one of Africa’s most established football sides.

APR FC head into the match after eliminating DR Congo’s FC Les Aigles du Congo in the previous round. Gen. Muganga urged the players to carry that momentum into their meeting with Zamalek, assuring them of the backing of the club’s leadership and supporters.

“We have the same confidence in you that we had before you eliminated Les Aigles du Congo. We expect you to perform well in this match too. Everyone here is ready to support you, and we expect you to deliver just as you did last time,” he said.

Gen. Muganga said the team had made improvements in recent matches and challenged the players to turn that progress into another positive result.

“What we expect from you is to make Rwandans everywhere proud. They are also ready to rally behind you,” he said, adding that the club’s management would continue to play its part in supporting the team.

Maj. Gen. Kagame, who led APR FC when they eliminated Zamalek in 2004, urged the players to prioritise teamwork, communication and mutual support.

“There is nothing else that brings victory apart from working together as a team. You should know when your teammate is struggling and step in to help. Talk among yourselves, share ideas and work towards one goal, knowing that we are all behind you,” he said.

Friday’s match will be the first leg of the two teams’ second-round tie, with APR FC seeking to secure an advantage before travelling to Egypt for the return leg on October 24.

Kick-off at Amahoro Stadium is scheduled for 6 p.m. local time. The winner over the two legs will advance to the group stage of the CAF Champions League.

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer .

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig :

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1 . For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM .

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket .

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket , rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR .

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace . If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions .

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset .

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard , explore the published result data , and reuse the study harness .

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.
